newsitem.title: USA: Conrail break-up details seen in 7-10 days.
newsitem.headline: Conrail break-up details seen in 7-10 days.

text.p: The heads of CSX Corp and Norfolk Southern Corp met with Pennsylvania Gov. Tom Ridge Monday and told him they expected to have a clearer picture of their planned division of Conrail Inc within a week to 10 days, officials said.

The political and business leaders in Monday's meeting also agreed to establish a working group to "negotiate" conditions for the support of Pennsylvania state and local leaders for the deal, which requires federal approval, Ridge spokesman Tim Reeves said.
"The word 'negotiate' was used," Reeves said. "As they (the railroads) seek to complete this transaction, Pennsylvania can be a helpful ally or a significant adversary."
He said Ridge told the railroads the state's position will depend on how its interests in preserving jobs and freight service in the state are met.
The negotiating group will begin meeting once the main terms of the Conrail division between CSX and Norfolk Southern have been clarified, he said.

CSX and Conrail, which is based in Philadelphia, on March 7 agreed to a $10.3 billion revised merger agreement that enables CSX to negotiate a division of Conrail with Norfolk Southern, which had pursued a hostile takeover battle for Conrail.
A CSX spokesman said talks between CSX and Norfolk Southern over dividing Conrail began last week, and the companies aimed to have more details on the deal in a week to 10 days.

"There will almost certainly be details left to handle, but I think the idea is, in a week to 10 days there will be enough detail agreed upon for a division of Conrail so that state and local communities will have a better idea of how this will affect them," the spokesman said.

Reeves said CSX Chairman John Snow and Norfolk Southern Chairman David Goode met for about one hour with Ridge, Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell and the heads of the state transportation department and the Delaware River Port Authority.

The political leaders' main interests in the deal are the fate of the more than 8,000 Conrail jobs in Pennsylvania and in the fate of freight service through the state, which affects even more jobs among companies reliant on the rail network, Reeves said.

"The preservation of those jobs is of paramount importance," he said. "More indirect, but just as important, is all the jobs in Pennsylvania that are dependent upon a competitive rail network in the state, and there are tens of thousands of jobs at stake in that regard."
